name: DeKalb County

actions.title: Emergency Moratorium on New Data Centers (Initial)
actions.summary: DeKalb County enacted an emergency moratorium halting acceptance of all new data center permit applications in unincorporated areas while zoning regulations were drafted.

actions.title: Data Center Moratorium Extended Through March 26, 2026
actions.summary: The Board of Commissioners extended the existing moratorium through March 26, 2026, prohibiting issuance of any permits, rezonings, or certificates of occupancy for new or expanded data centers in unincorporated DeKalb County.

actions.title: Data Center Text Amendment (Zoning Regulations) Proposed
actions.summary: A draft text amendment defining five size categories of data centers and restricting them to industrial zones with 500-foot residential setbacks, 750-foot park setbacks, and a half-mile transit-stop buffer was ultimately denied by the Board of Commissioners in June 2026.

actions.title: Moratorium Extended 100 Days Through September 30, 2026
actions.summary: After the text amendment failed, the Board extended the moratorium an additional 100 days through September 30, 2026, to allow more time to finalize permanent data center regulations.

contextBlurb: DeKalb County has been at the center of Georgia's data center regulatory wave, maintaining a continuous moratorium since July 2025 while drafting comprehensive zoning standards. Community groups including the DeKalb Coalition and Renew DeKalb participated actively across multiple public hearings over more than a year. The county's proposed text amendment, which included strict setbacks and transit-proximity limits, was ultimately denied by commissioners in June 2026, prompting yet another moratorium extension.

name: Fayette County / City of Fayetteville

actions.title: City of Fayetteville Moratorium on New Data Centers
actions.summary: Fayetteville enacted an initial moratorium on new data center development after intense community opposition to the existing QTS hyperscale campus, setting the stage for a permanent ordinance change.

actions.title: Fayetteville Ordinance 26-0-12: Permanent Ban on New Data Centers
actions.summary: The Fayetteville City Council adopted Ordinance 26-0-12, removing data centers from all zoning districts in the city's Unified Development Ordinance, effectively implementing a permanent citywide ban on new data centers.

actions.title: Crow Holdings Data Center Proposal Denied and Withdrawn
actions.summary: A new data center proposal from developer Crow Holdings was denied by the city's Planning & Zoning Commission in January 2026, and the company withdrew its appeal in March 2026 following the citywide ban.

contextBlurb: Fayette County became a flashpoint for Georgia's data center debate after QTS broke ground in 2023 on a 615-acre, 6.2-million-square-foot hyperscale campus — the first of its kind in the state. Residents discovered QTS had consumed 29 million gallons of unmetered water over 15 months, fueling public outrage. Community pressure, including packed planning meetings with over 100 attendees, led Fayetteville to ultimately ban all new data centers in every zoning district as of March 5, 2026.

name: Coweta County

actions.title: 180-Day Moratorium on Data Center Development
actions.summary: The Coweta County Board of Commissioners unanimously adopted a 180-day moratorium on data center development, prompted by the proposed $17 billion 'Project Sail' campus and a petition signed by 1,750 residents.

actions.title: Data Center Ordinance Enacted
actions.summary: Coweta County adopted a new data center ordinance at the end of 2025 permitting facilities in light and heavy industrial zones with strict requirements on location, buffering, design, noise, lighting, traffic, and utility capacity.

actions.title: Residents File Lawsuit Over Project Sail Rezoning (Environmental Review)
actions.summary: A group of Coweta County residents filed a lawsuit in Superior Court seeking to void the county's rezoning approval for the 'Project Sail' data center campus, alleging violations of the county's own ordinances, state law, and residents' constitutional rights.

contextBlurb: Coweta County faced intense pressure beginning in 2025 from Atlas Development's proposed 'Project Sail,' a 13-building, 800+ acre data center campus near Newnan estimated to consume 750–950 MW of power and three billion gallons of water annually. The county imposed a 180-day moratorium and eventually passed an ordinance in December 2025, but community opposition continued with a 2026 lawsuit challenging the rezoning. As of mid-2026 the county was also weighing a second moratorium as five more data centers were proposed.

name: Clayton County

actions.title: 120-Day Moratorium on Data Center Approvals
actions.summary: The Clayton County Board of Commissioners unanimously approved Resolution 2025-193 placing a moratorium on new data center approvals, rezonings, and permits through December 31, 2025, in response to resident concerns about rapid data center growth.

contextBlurb: Clayton County, home to a high concentration of industrial corridors, enacted a moratorium in September 2025 after two data centers were approved within the prior year and residents raised concerns about electromagnetic fields and water supplies. The moratorium was sponsored by Vice Chair Alaina Reaves, who cited the need to strategically plan data center locations before further growth. Clayton County's action was cited as a neighboring influence that helped Fayetteville activists secure their own data center ban.

name: Troup County

actions.title: Data Center Moratorium Enacted (First)
actions.summary: Troup County enacted an initial data center moratorium in September 2025 alongside Clayton, Lamar, and Pike counties to pause approvals while developing regulatory standards.

actions.title: Moratorium Extended 90 Days (Third Extension)
actions.summary: Troup County extended its data center moratorium for a third 90-day period through June 14, 2026, as the draft ordinance requiring special-use permits was not yet ready for a final vote.

actions.title: Data Center Ordinance Enacted with 1,500-Foot Setback and Height Cap
actions.summary: Troup County commissioners unanimously approved a 17-page data center ordinance requiring a 1,500-foot setback from sensitive receptors, a 40-foot height cap, mandatory special-use permits in industrial zones, Tier 4 diesel generators, public sewer connection, and on-site noise testing.

contextBlurb: Troup County's regulatory response was driven by proposed mega-projects including Google's 'Project Pegasus' in LaGrange and the $6 billion 'Project West' (whose developers were denied annexation into LaGrange). After three consecutive moratorium extensions spanning more than eight months, the county passed one of Georgia's most restrictive ordinances, featuring a 1,500-foot setback and 40-foot height cap. Community group Troup County Anti-Data Center Coalition participated throughout the drafting process and praised the county's ordinance as stronger than neighboring LaGrange's.

name: Athens-Clarke County

actions.title: Temporary Emergency Moratorium on New Data Centers
actions.summary: The Athens-Clarke County Commission adopted a temporary emergency moratorium on new data center establishments while the Planning Department developed zoning and land-use standards for eventual commission review.

actions.title: Commission Considers Moratorium Extension and Proposed Zoning Regulations
actions.summary: As of April 7, 2026, Athens-Clarke County commissioners were weighing whether to extend the data center moratorium or adopt proposed planning commission regulations requiring closed-loop cooling and specific zoning restrictions, amid 10+ hours of public debate.

contextBlurb: Athens-Clarke County imposed an emergency data center moratorium in late 2025 as concerns over water use, power demand, and rising utility costs dominated community conversation. By April 2026, commissioners faced a choice between extending the pause or adopting draft regulations that would require closed-loop water recycling and specific siting restrictions. State Representative Spencer Frye (D-Athens) was simultaneously pursuing legislation to eliminate state tax incentives for the data center industry.

name: Glynn County

actions.title: Joint Planning Commission Recommends 120-Day Moratorium
actions.summary: Members of both the Islands and Mainland Planning Commissions voted unanimously to recommend a 120-day moratorium to strengthen proposed data center zoning language, but the Board of Commissioners rejected this recommendation.

actions.title: New Zoning Ordinance Enacted Permitting Data Centers with Weak Standards
actions.summary: Glynn County commissioners unanimously adopted a 235-page zoning ordinance that permits data centers on lots of 50 acres or more with only a 50-foot setback and no noise or water-use standards, over objections from environmental groups who called the protections inadequate.

contextBlurb: Glynn County bucked the restrictive trend seen across most of Georgia by proactively permitting data centers in a new 235-page zoning code update, even though no data center proposals had yet been received. Environmental groups including One Hundred Miles argued the ordinance's 50-foot setback (far below the recommended 200–500 feet), and the absence of noise, water, or power-use standards left residents vulnerable. Both planning commissions unanimously urged a 120-day moratorium to strengthen the rules, but the Board of Commissioners overruled them and adopted the ordinance as written.

name: Muscogee County (Columbus)

actions.title: Technology Overlay Zoning Ordinance Proposed for Project Ruby
actions.summary: Following community uproar over the proposed 650 MW, $5.18 billion 'Project Ruby' hyperscale data center on nearly 900 acres, Columbus Consolidated Government began drafting a bespoke 'technology overlay' zoning ordinance rather than classifying the site as standard industrial, with a first reading scheduled for June 2, 2026.

contextBlurb: Columbus faced intense neighborhood opposition after Project Ruby — a proposed 650 MW hyperscale data center on 900 acres in the northeast corner of Muscogee County — was announced in February 2026. Rather than applying standard industrial zoning, Choose Columbus and the Columbus Consolidated Government opted to create a novel 'technology overlay' zoning category tailored to large-scale digital infrastructure, with a first ordinance reading set for June 2026. The project represents one of the largest proposed data center investments in Georgia history at $5.18 billion.
